analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top tax rate on business income to 25% and lets businesses deduct new investments immediately.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from January 2016 until the Congress ended, with 29 of 247 House Republicans signed on and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap the tax rate on all business income at 25%, down from a 35% corporate top rate and 39.6% top individual rate, and let businesses write off equipment, buildings, and other purchases in full the year they buy them. It would stop taxing profits U.S. companies earn abroad, repeal the corporate minimum tax and every business tax credit, and phase out the deduction for business interest over ten years. It would also tax individuals' interest income at the lower rate applied to dividends and capital gains.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of profitable businesses, corporations, and high-income investors gain the most: business income would never be taxed above 25%, corporate profits earned abroad would be untaxed, and interest income would move to the lower capital-gains rate. Highly profitable firms that buy a lot of equipment gain from immediate expensing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Business owners, corporations, and high-income investors

how_it_helps.text: Caps the tax rate on net business income for both individuals and corporations at 25%, with corporations paying only 15% on their first $50,000.
Lets businesses deduct the full cost of property, equipment, inventory, and services in the year of purchase, replacing the depreciation system.
Stops taxing income U.S. businesses earn from trade or business outside the United States, and charges a one-time 5% toll on accumulated foreign earnings instead of the old system.
Taxes individuals' interest income, reduced by interest paid, at the same rate as dividends and capital gains rather than ordinary income rates.
Repeals the corporate alternative minimum tax and expands relief for net operating losses, allowing a five-year carryback and an indefinite carryforward with interest.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect far less from business and capital income, and unless offset, the lost revenue has to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. Wage earners would keep paying their full ordinary rates while business and capital income is capped at 25%, shifting the relative burden toward people paid in wages. Highly indebted companies and financial institutions would lose the interest deduction and face a one-time transition tax on their claims.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a large gap between the 25% cap on business income and ordinary wage rates, giving professionals and owners a strong incentive to recharacterize salary as business income; the bill's own text concedes the risk by requiring that pass-through wages be 'reasonable for the service rendered' to be deductible.

It repeals every business tax credit and dozens of targeted deductions, including the research and experimentation credit, energy-efficient commercial building deductions, and clean-fuel vehicle provisions, removing incentives that industries and energy programs rely on.

It bars deduction of business interest after a ten-year transition, which raises financing costs for leveraged companies, real estate operations, and banks, and imposes a one-time 25% tax on financial institutions' net claims against non-business customers.
Exempting foreign business income from U.S. tax removes a major check on shifting profits and operations abroad, with only a one-time 5% toll on earnings accumulated before 2015.

The bill was never scored or debated in committee, so its revenue effects, including the cost of five-year loss carrybacks, transition basis deductions, and the interest phase-out, were never laid out for the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a deep, permanent rate cut for business and capital income while leaving wage income taxed at full ordinary rates, and it would make foreign profits untaxed. It has genuine virtues a fair critic should acknowledge: immediate expensing ends a notoriously arbitrary depreciation system, repealing special credits and LIFO accounting simplifies the code, and ending the interest deduction reduces the tax code's bias toward debt. But the offsets are partial and transition costs are heavy, and the bill was never scored, so nobody could say what it would do to federal revenue. On balance the gains flow overwhelmingly to owners of capital, and the burden of making up revenue would fall on taxpayers whose income stays at ordinary rates, mostly wage earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 13, 2016, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Representative Devin Nunes introduced the bill with 27 original cosponsors on January 13, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill picked up 29 Republican cosponsors in total and no Democratic cosponsors.
No hearing, markup, or floor action is recorded; the last entry in the action history is the referral to Ways and Means.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died without ever being scored or debated.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing corporate and individual tax structure, including its higher top rates on business income, its tax credits, and the interest deduction, stayed in place, and no revenue was cut from business and capital taxation. Wage earners were spared the prospect of a larger share of the tax burden.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing tax structure; no business tax cuts happened

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Republicans, amounting to 29 of the 247 House Republicans, and no Democrat supported it; the bill stalled in a committee chaired by a Republican, so partisan breakdown mattered less than the lack of committee action.

industries.note: A permanent 25% cap on business income, a 15% rate on the first $50,000 of corporate income, and immediate expensing would sharply cut taxes on business profits, while the wage income of ordinary workers would remain at full ordinary rates, shifting the relative burden toward them.

Switching to a territorial system means foreign business income would face no U.S. tax, removing the current check on booking profits abroad; only a one-time 5% toll applies to old accumulated earnings.

They would lose the business interest deduction and pay a one-time 25% tax on net claims against non-business customers, but interest income their customers earn would move to the lower capital-gains rate, a cut for savers.

The bill repeals the research credit and every energy-related deduction and credit, including for energy-efficient buildings, clean-fuel vehicles, and refineries, trading incentives for a lower flat rate.
